source_text: His compressi erumpunt dicere: (sufficit unicum hoc opus deo nostro, quod hominem liberauit summa et praecipua bonitate sua et omnibus locustis anteponenda\'. o deum maiorem, cuius tam magnum opus non potuit inueniri quam in homine dei minoris! enimuero prius est, ut eum probes esse per quae deum probari oportet, per opera, tunc deinde per beneficia. primo enim quaeritur, an sit, et ita, qualis sit. alterum de operibus, alterum de beneficiis dinoscetur. ceterum non quia liberasse dicitur hominem, ideo esse eum constat, sed si esse constiterit, tunc et liberasse dicetur, ut et an liberauerit constet, quia potuerit et esse et non liberasse. quomodo ergo, quia liberasse dicetur, etiam esse credetur, cum potuerit et esse et non liberasse? . Nunc, in isto articulo ab ignoti dei quaestione deducto si satis constitit tam nihil illum condidisse quam debuisse condidisse, uti cognosceretur ex operibus, quia si fuisset, cognosci debuisset, et utique a primordio rerum, — deum enim non decuisset latuisse — regrediar necesse est ad originem quaestionis dei ignoti, ut ceteros quoque ramulos eius excutiam. primo enim quaeri oportebit, qui postea se protulerit in notitiam cur postea et non a primordio rerum quibus utique necessarius, qua deus, et quidem necessarior quo melior latere non debuit. non enim potest dici non fuisse aut materiam aut causam cognoscendi deum, cum et homo a primordio esset in saeculo, cui nunc subuenit, et malitia creatoris, aduersus quam ut bonus subuenit. igitur aut ignorauit et causam et materiam suae reuelationis necessariae aut dubitanit ++ aut non potuit aut noluit. omnia haec deo indigna, maxime optimo. sed et hunc locum alibi implebimus exprobratione serae reuelationis, sicut nunc sola demonstratione.
pass_a_gloss: These compressed ones burst forth to say: (it is enough this one work of our God, that He liberated man by His supreme and principal goodness, and to be preferred before all places). Oh God greater, whose so great work could not be found except in the man of the lesser God! For indeed first, it is necessary to prove Him to be God through those things by which God ought to be proven, through works, then afterwards through benefits. For first it is sought, whether He is, and thus, what kind He is. One thing will be discerned from works, another from benefits. Moreover, not because it is said that He liberated man, therefore it is established that He is, but if it is established that He is, then He will also be said to have liberated, so that it may also be established whether He liberated, because He was able both to be and not to liberate. How therefore, because it is said that He liberated, is He also believed to be, when He was able both to be and not to liberate? Now, in this article, having been led away from the question of the unknown God, if it is sufficiently established that He neither created anything nor ought to have created, so that He might be known from works, because if He had been, He ought to have been known, and certainly from the beginning of things, — for it was not fitting for God to have been hidden — it is necessary to return to the origin of the question of the unknown God, so that I may also shake off the other branches of it. For first it will be necessary to ask, He who afterwards presented Himself to knowledge, why afterwards and not from the beginning of things, for which certainly He was necessary, since He is God, and indeed more necessary, the better He ought not to have been hidden. For it cannot be said that there was not either matter or cause for knowing God, since both man was from the beginning in the world, whom He now assists, and the malice of the creator, against which, as good, He assists. Therefore, either He ignored and the cause and matter of His necessary revelation, or He doubted, or He was not able, or He did not wish. All these things are unworthy of God, especially the best. But also we will fill up this place elsewhere with the reproach of the late revelation, just as now with the sole demonstration.

pass_b_english: They burst out of their corner and say: "One single work is enough for our God: He freed humanity by His supreme, paramount goodness — a work to be preferred to all places." (The manuscript actually reads 'locusts', but the absurdity is theirs.) Oh, a greater God! — whose work is so great it cannot be found anywhere except in the man of the lesser God! But the order of proof is backwards. First you have to prove He is God through the standard — His works — then, and only then, through His benefits. First you ask whether He exists, and then what kind of God He is. Existence is settled by works; character by benefits. You don't establish His existence simply because He is said to have freed humanity; you establish His existence first, and then you can say He freed humanity — so that it also becomes established whether He actually did free anyone, since He was capable both of existing and of not freeing. How, then, can He be believed to exist just because He is said to have freed, when He was capable both of existing and of not freeing?

Now, in this very article — drawn away from the question of the unknown God — if it is sufficiently established that He neither created anything nor ought to have created, so that He might be known through His works (because if He had existed, He ought to have been known, and certainly from the beginning of things — for it was not fitting for God to have stayed hidden) — we must go back to the origin of the question of the unknown God so that I can shake off its other branches as well. First it will be necessary to ask: He who presented Himself to knowledge only later, why later and not from the beginning of things, for which He was certainly necessary, since He is God, and indeed all the more necessary, because the better He is, the less He ought to have been hidden? It cannot be said that there was neither material nor cause for knowing God, since both humanity was in the world from the beginning — the very humanity He now assists — and the malice of the Creator, against which, as good, He assists. Therefore, either He ignored both the cause and the material of His necessary revelation, or He doubted, or He was unable, or He was unwilling. All of these are unworthy of God, especially the best God. But we will fill out this point elsewhere with the reproach of His late revelation, just as now we settle it with sheer demonstration.
notes: The original Latin text contains 'locustis' which seems to be a corruption, and the translation has been adjusted to 'locis' based on semantic context.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex logical structure of the Latin text, particularly the distinction between 'esse' (to be/existence) and 'liberare' (to free/liberate). Pass B correctly identifies and notes the OCR/manuscript error 'locustis' (locusts) vs 'locis' (places) in the source. The translation of the conditional and causal clauses preserves the author's argument regarding the necessity of God's revelation.
source: 'locustis', English: 'to be preferred before all places'
